entry.title: MIRRA: Fast, High-Fidelity Molecular Generation with Chemistry-Informed Discrete Flow Matching
entry.summary: Fast, high-fidelity molecular generation requires accurate chemical choices and efficient sampling. Chemical building blocks reduce graph size, but make each node a choice among tens of thousands of related identities. We introduce MIRRA (Molecular Identity Representation, Refresh and Assembly), a discrete flow-matching generator that learns from chemical knowledge and evaluates identity probabilities only when needed, while keeping every identity in its vocabulary available. Chemical features share information across related blocks, and learned identity corrections distinguish them in molecular context. By deciding which positions will refresh before computing their probabilities, the sampler avoids unused predictions while preserving each sampling transition. Against the strongest baselines in each task, MIRRA reduces chemical and graph distribution errors on ZINC250k by 29-31% and 53-60%, respectively, with generation up to 8.6 times faster. Property targeting yields an estimated 7.8-20.8 times more distinct novel hits per second. On a held-out polymer test set, MIRRA achieves 100% periodic validity with known chain topology, versus 57.0% for a polymer variational autoencoder. These results demonstrate fast, high-fidelity generation with the full chemical vocabulary available throughout sampling.

entry.title: Principles and Techniques for Agentic Research in Experimental Physics
entry.summary: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in physics research is increasingly common, yet few guidelines exist for its effective use. Starting with a principles-based approach, we outline a set of ten requirements for collaborative AI agents in experimental physics, spanning scientific norms, effective agent use, and domain expertise. We take a human-centered approach in which agents act as collaborators that amplify rather than replace the expertise of a human researcher (user) who directs the work and is responsible for its results. We then present a framework designed to enforce these requirements, detailing methods for improving off-the-shelf behavior of large language models (LLMs) with custom scaffolding and describing general-purpose scientific workflows and skills. In particular, we highlight the power of closed-loop campaigns where agents work iteratively toward a well-defined goal. We demonstrate the potential of this mode of research through six case studies in experimental physics, covering device design, hardware control, neural network optimization, physical model identification, and data analysis. All six case studies result in useful work products that add utility to our research, including a neural network architecture and solid-state quantum defect photodynamic model that substantially outperform our published work; a microwave waveguide design that extends a published design concept to a fabrication-ready device meeting our experimental constraints; a quantum control pulse sequence candidate that improves simulated performance by more than an order of magnitude; commissioning of an NMR spectrometer to $\sim$1~Hz frequency precision on live hardware; and finally a data-fitting pipeline that achieves, to our knowledge, the first reconstruction of the Ising microstate of an artificial spin-ice array from diffraction-limited magnetic imaging.

entry.title: A Fully Discrete, Mass-Conservative Adaptive Discontinuous Spectral-Element Method for the One-Dimensional Richards Equation in Mixed Form
entry.summary: We present and analyze a spatially and temporally adaptive high-order method for the one-dimensional Richards equation describing vertical water transport in unsaturated soil, with an emphasis on resolving sharp wetting fronts while satisfying a fully discrete water mass balance. The spatial discretization uses an arbitrary-order local discontinuous Galerkin spectral-element formulation with collocated Legendre-Gauss-Lobatto quadrature, and the time integration is based on a high-order Rosenbrock-Wanner method. We focus primarily on the mixed formulation of the Richards equation, which advances water content as the conserved variable while evaluating the nonlinear diffusion operator in terms of pressure head; the resulting fully discrete scheme satisfies the water mass balance in exact arithmetic, independent of spatial resolution and time step size, including under spatial and temporal adaptivity. In contrast, the pressure-head formulation advances pressure head through a nonlinear capacity function and satisfies the corresponding conservation identity only at the semi-discrete level. Numerical experiments examine convergence through spatial and temporal refinement studies, with mass conservation assessed under spatial and temporal adaptivity using the solver flux output method (SFOM). The SFOM results confirm machine-precision mass conservation for the mixed formulation, whereas the pressure-head formulation exhibits mass balance errors above roundoff. Moreover, in the temporal refinement studies, the mixed formulation yields more accurate solutions than the pressure-head formulation for a prescribed time step size. The combination of high-order accuracy, spatial and temporal adaptivity, and fully discrete mass conservation makes the proposed mixed-form discontinuous spectral-element method a promising approach for simulating unsaturated flow in next-generation land models.

entry.title: Honeycomb Crystal in a Mass-Asymmetric Electron-Hole Bilayer
entry.summary: A two-dimensional electron gas in a uniform neutralizing background forms a triangular Wigner crystal at low density. In a strongly mass-asymmetric electron-hole bilayer, localized heavy holes instead provide a nonuniform positive background that supports an electron crystal at densities two orders of magnitude higher than for a homogeneous electron gas in the same material. Here we show that correlated mobile electrons can overturn the preference for triangular order, stabilizing a honeycomb electron-hole crystal. Using the powerful real-space neural-network variational Monte Carlo in the Born-Oppenheimer limit with fixed holes, we find that increasing the density drives a transition from a triangular electron-hole crystal to a honeycomb crystal, which eventually melts into itinerant electrons coexisting with the honeycomb or the triangular hole lattice at fixed interlayer separation. Relative to triangular order, honeycomb order emerges when gains in electronic kinetic energy and electron-hole attraction outweigh its higher intralayer Coulomb repulsion, a threshold never reached in the rigid point-dipole model. Moreover, the honeycomb hole lattice supports paramagnetic, antiferromagnetic, and stripe-ordered spin states. Complex polarization indicates a metal-insulator transition, while the states on the honeycomb hole lattice are consistent with a stripe-ordered Dirac semimetal and paramagnetic or antiferromagnetic Mott insulators via mapping to the half-filled Hubbard model. We further propose a BLG/hBN/WS$_2$-WSe$_2$ heterostructure as a platform for the predicted honeycomb crystal, at an experimentally feasible density $n\sim10^{11}~\text{cm}^{-2}$.

entry.title: First-Principles Calculations of the Electron-Hole-Pair Creation Energy in Semiconductors and Dielectrics
entry.summary: We present first-principles calculations of the electron-hole-pair creation energy in semiconductors and dielectrics, focusing in particular on AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2. We have employed density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the band structure, density-functional perturbation theory to obtain the phonon dispersion, and time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) to calculate the electron energy loss function (via the dielectric function). We performed full-band Monte Carlo simulations of electron thermalization for energies up to ~100 eV and calculated the average energy required to excite an electron-hole pair. We calculated pair-creation energies of approximately 12.2, 6.5, 7.3, 3.10, and 16.7 eV/pair for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2, respectively. These values are in good agreement with measured data, with the largest discrepancy being that of Si (about 14.9% lower than the accepted experimental value of ~3.6 eV/pair). To improve the agreement for Si, we used the GW approach and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) to calculate the quasiparticle shifts of the electronic band structure and the dielectric function, respectively. Finally, using the GW/BSE data, we calculated a creation energy of ~3.50 eV/pair. We find that the marked improvement in the accuracy of the calculated creation energy, when using the GW/BSE approach, is primarily attributable to the slight decrease in the magnitude of the electron energy-loss function when using the GW/BSE approach for energies below ~10-15 eV. Overall, it is clear that the competition between phonon emission and ionization near the intersection of the phonon scattering and ionization rates is largely responsible for determining the value of the creation energy, with the other major factor being the location and shape of the plasmon peak in the energy-loss function.

entry.title: First-fracture kinetics in periodic chains: from free-energy landscapes and dynamical recrossing to absolute rates
entry.summary: The nearly collinear configuration of highly stretched polymer chains before fracture motivates one-dimensional models. At fixed extension, stretching one bond redistributes length among the others, coupling rupture to the whole chain. In this work, I develop a framework for fracture-healing rates in periodic Morse chains, combining deterministic theories, equilibrium simulations and a quasi-deterministic approach using equilibrium fluxes and barrier-top trajectories. Constrained-partition calculations closely reproduce simulated populations and intact-state tensions. An intact-reservoir potential of mean force (PMF) supplies the first-fracture surface probability, while recrossing corrects the attempt flux without a rate-fitted prefactor. Independent rate tests identify an operational chain-length boundary for accurate two-state kinetics; failed-return durations decrease relative to population relaxation as chains grow. Kramers-Grote-Hynes (KGH), nonlinear reactive-flux and equilibrium rates show excellent agreement in this regime. KGH predicts rates away from coexistence and a chain-dependent local activation length dominated by the barrier response. Rates decrease approximately exponentially before declining more gently for longer chains: barrier growth dominates, additional fracture sites partly compensate, and transmission varies more weakly. Beyond coexistence, long chains can fracture practically irreversibly because healing becomes too rare to observe. Projected committor crossings, where the configuration-averaged probability of reaching the fractured core first is one half, lie near site-PMF maxima, although configurations at equal bond length retain different fracture probabilities. Multiple fractures remain negligible near coexistence through at least $N=50$. The framework could supply state-dependent rates to mesoscopic fracture models of polymer networks.

entry.title: Development of a Particle Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook Method for Rarefied Monatomic Gas Mixtures
entry.summary: The Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method has long served as a reliable numerical approach for simulating rarefied and non-equilibrium gas flows. Its computational cost, however, increases rapidly as the flow approaches the near-continuum regime. This limitation has motivated the development of kinetic model equations that replace binary collisions with simplified relaxation processes. This paper presents a particle multi-relaxation unified BGK (UBGK) model for monatomic gas mixtures. The model retains pairwise species relaxation and determines the target velocity, temperature, shear stress, and heat flux by matching the corresponding production terms to those of the Boltzmann equation. A stochastic particle algorithm is developed. The model is implemented in SPARTA, and two validation problems are considered: homogeneous relaxation and a Mach 3 flow over a cylinder. In both cases, the UBGK solution reproduces the DSMC reference behavior, including species-dependent relaxation and non-equilibrium shock structure.

entry.title: Thermal aliases in quantum noise: sampling clocks and pulse widths
entry.summary: Can collective quantum-noise measurements distinguish different mode temperatures from one common temperature when the coupling spectrum is unknown? For stationary Gaussian oscillator environments, we derive a sharp bandwidth threshold for an exact thermal alias on the integer-time sampling lattice. The threshold depends on temperature order through the quantum response. For frequencies within the first alias period, fixing sufficient integer-time correlations makes one additional fractional-time fluctuation observation enough to exclude every common-temperature fit. A calibrated second pulse width provides another route through the same collective port: both widths must probe one spectrum and retain their measured variance scales. For a specified two-mode example, continuous-frequency certificates cover all common temperatures and uncertainty in a shared pulse ramp. A binary-readout protocol combines randomly interleaved matched references with collective-variance and coherence checks to handle Gaussian oscillator loss and predictable readout drift. The selected fractional-clock and two-width designs require approximately $3.8\times10^7$ and $1.6\times10^8$ outcomes for at most 5\% type-I error and at least 95\% power on the stated alternative class. These theoretical and numerical acquisition guarantees assume independently validated preparation, spectral support and control specifications; validation costs are additional. The result identifies which new observation makes thermal-model testing informative when mode-resolved access is unavailable.

entry.title: Exact Gaussian--Hermite closure of the mapping quantum--classical Liouville equation
entry.summary: In the Meyer--Miller--Stock--Thoss mapping representation, the Liouville operator of the quantum--classical Liouville equation contains an excess coupling term in addition to the Poisson bracket. Neglecting this term yields the Poisson bracket mapping equation (PBME). We expand the mapping dependence of the density in Hermite functions about the Gaussian factor common to all physical mapping densities. In this basis, the excess coupling term acts purely as a raising operator and exactly cancels the raising contribution generated by the back--reaction force. Consequently, the exact dynamics does not generate higher Hermite orders and closes on a finite, sparse system of equations for the coefficient fields. Within the physical sector, these equations reduce to the subsystem quantum--classical Liouville equation. In contrast, the PBME retains the raising contribution of the force, modifying the back reaction within the physical sector while continuously generating higher Hermite orders. For Tully's dual avoided crossing model, direct propagation of the coefficient equations confirms this finite closure and agrees with independent solutions of the subsystem equation. Comparison with converged full quantum dynamics further shows that, across all regimes examined, the PBME is less accurate than the quantum--classical description for populations, coherences, and momentum distributions.

entry.title: Bayesian Inversion Beyond the Generator's Range: Reducing Non-physical Constraints from Generative Neural Networks
entry.summary: To address non-uniqueness in geophysical inversions, Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are often used to parameterise geological or other prior information in a lower-dimensional space (the so-called latent space), thereby reducing the number of inversion parameters. However, the training samples that represent this information are then always incorrect, because Earth structure is not intrinsically low-dimensional, and all GNNs are subject to training errors. Consequently, even when solutions are mapped back to the original higher-dimensional space, they inherit this imperfection and remain restricted to a low-dimensional manifold. From a mathematical point of view, latent space inversion thus fails fundamentally: generally, it can not even reproduce the best, higher-dimensional approximation to the true Earth. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an `escaping prior' distribution, which provides the necessary freedom to find solutions beyond the manifold of GNN-generated solutions, while still using the GNN as a guide. We use a hierarchical Bayesian approach to adapt the strength of prior information to the observed data and synthetic forward function $\textit{a posteriori}$. We illustrate our method on low-dimensional problems where the escaping prior is defined over a 1D manifold in 2D space. We then compare our approach with standard latent space and model space inversions using a uniform prior distribution in synthetic tomography problems, ranging from simple to more geologically realistic cases. Furthermore, we tested scenarios where the true solution is either far from or close to the manifold. In each case, our escaping prior shows significantly better results than the alternatives. It results in solutions beyond each GNN's generative capabilities, solutions which include the best possible model, and clearly demonstrates the limitations of latent space inversion.

entry.title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling
entry.summary: Poorly soluble species can have mean populations below one in small systems such as nanopores. In this regime, the grand-potential minimum, which identifies the most probable particle number, differs from the ensemble-averaged solute loading. We use grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling (GCWLS) to calculate the density of states $Ω(N_\mathrm{A}, N_\mathrm{B})$ for a binary Lennard-Jones mixture of solute B in solvent A, both in bulk and in slit pores. One set of GCWLS simulations gives ensemble averages over a range of chemical potentials, whereas conventional grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation requires a separate simulation at each state point. Independent GCMC simulations confirm the GCWLS ensemble averages. The solvent number distribution is nearly Gaussian, whereas the dilute solute distribution is skewed and Poisson-like. The most probable solute number therefore lies below the ensemble-averaged loading $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle$ and is zero whenever $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle<1$. Reading the solute loading from the grand-potential minimum underestimates it and can falsely indicate that no solute is present. Defining the oversolubility as $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}=x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}/x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$, where $x_\mathrm{B}$ is the solute mole fraction, we find $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}\approx12$ in a pore of 3.5 particle diameters width when both wall interactions are repulsive. Adding wall-solute attraction moderately raises it to $\approx13$, whereas wall-solvent attraction lowers it to $\approx3.4$. This comparison shows that the wall-solvent interaction controls most of the enhancement. As the pore widens, $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}$ decreases toward unity. In bulk and in nanopores alike, the solubility of poorly soluble species should be obtained from ensemble averages rather than from grand-potential minima.

entry.title: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method for the shallow water equations on Cartesian grids: mass conservation and wetting and drying over variable topography
entry.summary: A ghost-cell immersed boundary method is proposed for the two-dimensional shallow water equations with a variable bed (topography), solved with an explicit Godunov-type finite volume scheme (unsplit second-order MUSCL, HLLC flux, hydrostatic reconstruction) on Cartesian grids. Ghost-cell methods leak mass through the wall. To find a robust and conservative treatment, eight constructions of the ghost values and a cut-cell form of the continuity equation were applied to seven test problems, which include wetting and drying on sloping beds and a laboratory dam break. In the resulting scheme, the ghost values are interpolated bilinearly at the image point; solid and dry nodes are excluded, and the weights of the remaining nodes are renormalized. Mass is conserved by solving the continuity equation in cut-cell form, while the momentum equations are left unchanged. The proposed scheme is about as accurate as the ghost-cell method without this modification and preserves a lake at rest whose shoreline crosses an immersed wall. Because only the continuity equation is modified, it avoids the treatment of the momentum equations on cut cells (wall pressure, cell merging) that a full cut-cell method requires.

entry.title: Supercell-enabled inverse design of boundary-state dispersion for group-velocity control in pseudomagnetic phononic crystals
entry.summary: Topological boundary states offer a platform for guided-wave propagation within bulk bandgaps. Their propagation characteristics depend not only on the spectral extent of the states but also on their dispersion within the operating bandwidth. A nearly linear dispersion provides more uniform group velocity across frequency, whereas a reduced slope enables slow-wave propagation. Despite advances in inverse design of prescribed dispersion relations and topological dispersion tuning, application-oriented characteristics of boundary-state dispersion have rarely been direct inverse-design objectives. Here, we develop a supercell-enabled, surrogate-assisted framework for the inverse design of boundary-state dispersion in a phononic crystal with pseudomagnetic fields. Area-preserving anisotropic deformation shifts the local Dirac points, and independent variation of 21 rows within the supercell provides distributed control over the boundary-state branch. A constraint-preserving surrogate reconstructs the dispersion from an initial frequency and positive frequency increments, with first- and second-difference losses introduced to capture local slope and curvature. Coupled with a genetic algorithm, the framework targets two prescribed-bandwidth design tasks: highly linear dispersion and slow-wave dispersion. For the former, finite-element verification yields relative group-velocity variations of 0.142% to 1.183% over prescribed bandwidths of 4% to 6%. For slow-wave designs, mean group velocities of 190 to 385 m/s are obtained over bandwidths of 0.2% to 0.8% while satisfying a 5% group-velocity variation limit. These results establish boundary-state dispersion as a direct inverse-design target beyond conventional bandwidth optimization, opening a flexible route to group-velocity control through application-oriented dispersion engineering over prescribed relative bandwidths.

entry.title: Nonlocal generalization of the Chapman-Enskog method and hydrodynamic equations. Nonlocal vorticity transport in a turbulent medium
entry.summary: The results from [Fluid Dyn 61, 20 (2026)], concerning the generalized Chapman-Enskog method and a nonlocal (i.e., non-diffusive, spatially integral) viscous stress tensor in the Navier-Stokes equation, are extended to the case of arbitrary gradients of not only hydrodynamic velocity but also temperature. The resulting equations simplify the description of tangential discontinuities and separated flows. For the specific case of an incompressible medium, a nonlocal vorticity transport equation is derived that is structurally identical to the Biberman-Holstein equation for resonant radiation transport in plasmas and gases. A power-law form has been determined for the velocity distribution function of long-free-path vorticity carriers that satisfies empirical Richardson t^3 law for the mean square of relative separation of a pair of particles in a turbulent liquid or gaseous medium.

entry.title: Self-Adaptive Model-Order Reduction for Shock-Dominated Problems
entry.summary: Projection-based model-order reduction (MOR) offers a promising approach for accelerating expensive full-order model (FOM) by constructing reduced-order models (ROMs) that retain the majority of FOM accuracy while significantly reducing the computational cost. However, conventional static ROMs, often following offline/online training strategy, can exhibit limited predictive capability for convection-dominated problems featuring strongly evolving physics such as shocks. Adaptive ROMs emerge as a promising alternative and address such limitation by dynamically updating the low-dimensional subspace during online simulation to track locally evolving system dynamics, thereby enabling accurate predictions even for shock-dominated flows. However, such online adaptation introduces additional computational overhead, and frequent basis and sampling-point updates can substantially reduce their computational advantage relative to their static counterpart. To reconcile this tradeoff, the current work introduces a self-adaptive MOR framework that dynamically constructs and deploys the most appropriate ROM formulation (either adaptive or static) on the fly according to the evolving characteristics of the solution. to achieve optimal computational efficiency while maintaining high modeling accuracy of the local physics during the online model execution. In this regard, the proposed framework seeks to exploit the advantages of both adaptive- and static-ROM approaches to achieve an optimal computational efficiency and predictive accuracy while reducing reliance on extensive offline training. The framework is developed and evaluated for modeling rotating detonation engines (RDEs), which provide a challenging test environment involving strongly convection-dominated, transient, and multiscale reacting-flow dynamics.

entry.title: Magpie: A Graphical Magnon Software
entry.summary: Magpie is a fully graphical linear spin-wave software which has its main focus on 3-d visualisation of magnetic models and magnon dispersion relations. The software is distributed under an open-source license and is written in high-performance, portable C++. Its modular architecture allows for a rapid development of new calculation modules and permits the inclusion into external applications. Included code generators ensure seamless interoperability with other linear spin-wave libraries.

entry.title: Kernel-Level Constant-Potential Molecular Dynamics in GROMACS
entry.summary: How charge rearranges within an electrode shapes the behavior of batteries, supercapacitors, and other electrochemical devices. Molecular simulations can capture this response by allowing the charge on each electrode atom to adjust to its surroundings, but repeatedly calculating these charges adds substantial computational cost. We present an open-source implementation of the constant-potential method in GROMACS that integrates these calculations into the program's optimized CPU and GPU routines. Comparisons with established codes validate the electrode charges, while charging, voltammetry, and impedance simulations demonstrate the response to changing electrical conditions. The implementation also supports electrodes that move or deform and models of finite metallic screening and electron spillover. In a pair of charged carbon nanotubes, allowing charge to move away from the facing surfaces reduces the repulsive force at contact by about half at an intermediate charge and keeps the pair bound where a uniform-charge model opens within the simulated time. These capabilities make the electrical response of electrodes accessible within GROMACS for studies of interfacial structure, charging dynamics, and electrode motion.

entry.title: Dual deconvolution multifocal fluorescence response matrix microscopy for aberration-free high-throughput super-resolution imaging
entry.summary: Fluorescence response matrix imaging enables separate computational correction of excitation and emission aberrations through dual deconvolution, but single-focus acquisition requires a large number of camera frames, limiting its practical use. Multifocal excitation can accelerate acquisition by recording many illumination positions in parallel, but denser foci also increase inter-focus crosstalk, which can bias the estimated excitation and emission optical transfer functions and degrade aberration correction. Here, we introduce high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging with adaptive multifocal illumination, in which the inter-focus spacing of the multifocal lattice is adjusted according to specimen-dependent crosstalk. A programmable digital micromirror device generates multifocal excitation lattices, and the resulting detector-resolved fluorescence responses are assembled into a two-coordinate fluorescence response matrix. Dual deconvolution separately estimates and corrects the excitation and emission optical transfer functions, and the aberration-corrected matrix is then combined in the spatial-frequency domain to reconstruct the aberration-free image. This strategy reduces the number of required camera frames by approximately three orders of magnitude, allowing response matrices with $\sim 10^6$ illumination positions to be acquired within seconds to a few minutes. The accelerated acquisition preserves the aberration-correction capability of dual deconvolution and achieves an estimated lateral resolution of $\sim$100 nm. Applied to heterogeneous mouse brain and kidney tissue, the method enables high-resolution, depth-resolved volumetric imaging while correcting specimen-dependent aberrations. Together, these results establish adaptive multifocal illumination as a practical route to high-throughput aberration-free fluorescence response matrix imaging.

entry.title: Data-Driven Discovery of a Hyperelastic Strain-Energy Function for Veins Using Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks
entry.summary: Veins are commonly subjected to altered mechanical loading in clinical settings such as vein grafting, arteriovenous fistula creation, and tissue-engineered vascular graft implantation, making accurate constitutive models of venous tissue clinically important. Venous mechanical behavior differs characteristically from that of arteries, and existing constitutive models struggle to simultaneously fit the circumferential and axial stress-stretch responses across vein types. Here, we present a constitutive artificial neural network (CANN) framework that discovers a compact, interpretable hyperelastic constitutive model from biaxial mechanical data across three types of veins (saphenous, jugular, and inferior vena cava). The framework incorporates an expanded candidate function library with structurally motivated terms representing progressive fiber recruitment and fiber-family interactions. Sobol sensitivity analysis, correlation-based pruning, and response-level family collapse were then used to reduce the discovered basis to a compact strain-energy density function (SEF). The resulting eight-term SEF achieved significantly higher fitting accuracy than established venous constitutive models across all three types of veins $(R^2>0.9, p<0.01)$. These findings establish a framework for constitutive model discovery in veins and propose a candidate constitutive form for further validation across larger, independent cohorts.

entry.title: BSMScanner: a lightweight framework for beyond-the-Standard-Model global fits
entry.summary: We present BSMScanner, a framework in which a beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) parameter scan is specified as a set of declarative YAML documents rather than written as a program. The user declares the free parameters and their priors, the mass matrices and the diagonalisations that act on them, the observables, the theory-validity conditions and the likelihood terms. The framework validates this specification, resolves it into a dependency graph and compiles it once into a typed C++ evaluation kernel, which is then driven by an independently chosen scanning engine: uniform sampling, two differential-evolution engines, or a staged basin-discovery orchestrator, optionally followed by Markov-chain posterior refinement. Flavour physics matrix diagonalisation, PMNS and CKM construction in fixed conventions, tabulated oscillation likelihoods and a library of common flavour observables are provided by the framework and imported by name, so that a model file contains only model-specific definitions; quantities without a closed form, such as a relic density, enter through a C++ or Python plugin interface. We describe the specification schema, the observable and likelihood library, the scanning engines and their configuration, and demonstrate the framework on six benchmark models with $4$ to $26$ free parameters, giving for each the specification, the scan configuration, the resulting best fit and analytic cross-checks of the result.

entry.title: A quantum algorithm for meshless lattice Boltzmann method with unitary interpolation
entry.summary: We present a mass-weighted meshless formulation for the shifted incompressible lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) whose streaming step is exactly unitary, combining with the Carleman embedding. In traditional meshless LBM, on a scattered node set the semi-Lagrangian streaming step is an interpolation, which is not unitary; a generic block encoding of this matrix therefore requires a normalization proportional to its sparsity and logarithmically many ancillas. To overcome the non-unitarity, we instead express the interpolation as the exponential exp(a Dx + b Dy) of mimetic derivative operators. Endowing each node with its Voronoi mass and applying a mass-weighted similarity transform renders these derivative operators skew-Hermitian by enforcing moment constraints together with low-wave number trigonometric differentiation conditions, so that the interpolation becomes exactly unitary. Such unitarization of interpolation leave the local collision step unchanged up to a rescaling of its quadratic term, where the same weights define the amplitude encoding of the distribution functions. For quasi-uniform node sets, the mass-weighting diagonal remains within a unit-order normalization that degrades only mildly as the Carleman truncation order grows, thereby mitigating the cost of block encoding. Numerical experiments on the Taylor Green vortex confirm that the method reproduces the full meshless LBM, with the velocity error decreasing as the Carleman order increases.

entry.title: A single LU~factorization approach to model reduction for linear system families with a quadratic matrix pencil
entry.summary: To solve a family of large linear systems where the system matrix depends on the family parameter quadratically, we propose a new solution approach. Our method employs the derivatives of solutions with respect to the parameter. It turns out that the accumulated solution derivatives of increasing order, evaluated at a single specially chosen parameter value, provide successively better approximations to solution subspaces for the whole linear system family. We show that the derivatives can be computed by a recurrence, involving, at each step, solving a linear system with the same matrix. Constructing an orthonormal basis for the subspace spanned by the derivatives then leads to an efficient solver where just a single (sparse) LU factorization (or a single preconditioner setup in an iterative scheme) suffices to solve the whole linear system family. We call the new method ODB (orthonormal derivative basis method). As shown in numerical tests, compared to conventional solution methods, the ODB method allows to drastically reduce computational costs.

entry.title: FDTD Model of Noise Pollution from an AI Data Center
entry.summary: The sudden growth in AI data centers is raising numerous environmental concerns. Low-frequency noise pollution is a concern for local residents, that may not just be an annoyance but also carry significant health impacts. An FDTD model of sound propagation over the topography near an AI data center is presented. The topography plays a large role in the level of noise pollution, with areas of sudden elevation on either side of the river near the AI data center more susceptible to high noise levels, while areas further afield largely protected from noise pollution by the topography. Understanding the role that topography plays in noise pollution, and capturing the noise pollution in specific topographies, can help identify areas where noise mitigation strategies might be best employed.

entry.title: Are implicit schemes needed in adaptive time stepping for PDEs?
entry.summary: Implicit time integration is the standard way to overcome the tight CFL time step restriction when solving nonstationary PDEs numerically. However, within an adaptive time accurate integration, the time step size selection is governed not only by stability but also by accuracy requirements. Therefore, an eligible question to ask is: is (unconditionally) stable implicit time stepping really needed if the time step is restricted by accuracy considerations anyway? And how much do we then lose (in terms of the time step size) when switching from the expensive implicit time stepping to stabilized explicit schemes? An answer to this question is also important because such a switch is often done when solving large scale nonstationary PDEs on massively parallel computers. This paper attempts to answer these questions by numerical tests for two particular adaptive time accurate settings: (i)~nonstationary convection-diffusion equations and (ii)~nonlinear heat equations.
